Welch's big realization was simple: why does LZ78 have to transmit `(0, 'A')` just to teach the decoder that the single byte `'A'` exists? Both computers already know beforehand that a byte can only ever hold one of $$256$$ possible single-symbol values ($$0$$ through $$255$$)!

By agreeing in advance that the first $$256$$ dictionary entries *already* hold every possible single byte, the encoder never has to transmit a `(code, raw character)` pair. An LZW stream consists of **100 percent dictionary code numbers** from start to finish.

questions.prompt: What does the compressed output stream of the Lempel–Ziv–Welch (LZW) algorithm consist of?
choices: A continuous sequence of dictionary code numbers with no explicit raw characters mixed in.
Alternating pairs of backward distance pointers and uncompressed RGB color triplets.
A pre-computed frequency table of the 100 most common pixel runs followed by raw bytes.
Plain English words describing the geometric shapes and gradients in the picture.
questions.explanation: By pre-populating the dictionary with all possible single-symbol roots, Terry Welch's LZW algorithm eliminated LZ78's explicit character field and transmitted only dictionary code numbers.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't an LZW encoder need to waste output tokens teaching the decoder about single-byte values the first time they appear?
choices: Single-byte values are never compressed and are sent over a separate second telephone line.
The LZW algorithm automatically deletes any single byte that does not repeat at least twice.
Both encoder and decoder pre-populate their starting dictionaries with all possible single-symbol values.
The user must type in a list of all single-byte values present in the picture before opening it.
questions.explanation: Because the set of possible single symbols (such as byte values 0–255) is known in advance, both sides initialize their dictionaries with those single-symbol roots before processing the first pixel.

chunks.title: GIF's Pre-Populated Root Table: Indices 0 through 255
chunks.content_markdown:
When Steve Wilhite adopted LZW for GIF87a in 1987, Welch's pre-populated dictionary fit GIF's $$8\text{-bit}$$ Color Lookup Table like a key in a lock.

In a standard $$256\text{-color}$$ GIF image, every pixel is a palette index between $$0$$ and $$255$$. Therefore, before reading a single pixel of the picture, both the GIF encoder and the GIF decoder silently initialize an **implicit pre-populated root table (indices 0–255)**:
- Dictionary Entry `0` $$=$$ single pixel of Palette Color `0`
- Dictionary Entry `1` $$=$$ single pixel of Palette Color `1`
- $$\dots$$
- Dictionary Entry `255` $$=$$ single pixel of Palette Color `255`

Why is the word **implicit** so important here? Because this starting table of $$256$$ single-pixel entries is built into the rules of GIF itself—it **never has to be written into the file**! Zero bytes of phone-line bandwidth are spent transmitting the dictionary.

questions.prompt: In a 256-color GIF file, what do LZW dictionary entries 0 through 255 represent at the start of compression?
choices: The 256 most common 10-pixel horizontal streaks found during a pre-scan of the image.
The 256 individual single-pixel palette indices from the Color Lookup Table.
The 256 ASCII text characters used to write the image creator's copyright notice.
The 256 telephone area codes supported by CompuServe's dial-up network.
questions.explanation: In a 256-color GIF, the root dictionary entries 0 through 255 correspond one-to-one with the 256 single-pixel palette indices.

questions.prompt: How many bytes inside a GIF file are spent storing the LZW dictionary table itself?
choices: 256 bytes, stored right after the Color Lookup Table at the top of the file.
4,096 bytes, appended as a mandatory footer at the very end of the file.
12,288 bytes, split evenly across the four interlaced passes of the image.
Zero bytes, because the starting root table is implicit and all new entries are rebuilt on the fly.
questions.explanation: A GIF file never stores or transmits the LZW dictionary; both sides start from the same implicit root table (0–255) and construct identical multi-pixel entries dynamically from the code stream.

chunks.title: Reserved Control Codes: Clear (256) and End of Information (257)
chunks.content_markdown:
If slots `0` through `255` hold all $$256$$ single-pixel colors, does the first multi-pixel dictionary phrase get assigned to slot `256`? Almost—but Steve Wilhite reserved two special slot numbers right above the root colors as traffic-control signals for the decoder: the **Clear code (256) and End-of-Information code (257)**.

Here is what those two reserved codes do in a $$256\text{-color}$$ GIF:
- **Code `256` (Clear Code):** Tells the decoder, *'Wipe out all learned multi-pixel phrases from slot `258` upward and reset the dictionary back to its clean initial state (slots `0`–`255`)!'* In fact, GIF encoders traditionally emit a `256` Clear code as the very first token of the image stream.
- **Code `257` (End of Information / EOI):** Tells the decoder, *'The pixel stream for this image is officially complete—stop decoding!'*

Because slots `0`–`255` are single pixels and slots `256`–`257` are reserved control codes, the **very first learned two-pixel phrase** in a $$256\text{-color}$$ GIF always goes into **Slot `258`**!

questions.prompt: In a 256-color GIF, what are LZW dictionary slots 256 and 257 reserved for, and which slot receives the very first learned multi-pixel phrase?
choices: Slots 256 and 257 are Clear and End-of-Information control codes; the first learned phrase goes into slot 258.
Slots 256 and 257 store pure black and pure white; the first learned phrase goes into slot 0.
Slots 256 and 257 store the image width and height; the first learned phrase goes into slot 512.
Slots 256 and 257 are unused padding; the first learned phrase overwrites slot 255.
questions.explanation: In an 8-bit (256-color) GIF, code 256 is the Clear code and code 257 is the End-of-Information (EOI) code, so newly learned multi-pixel strings begin at index 258.

questions.prompt: What action does a GIF decoder take the moment it reads a Clear code (256) in the compressed LZW stream?
choices: It erases the user's monitor screen to solid black and restarts the file download.
It discards all learned dictionary entries (258 and above) and resets the dictionary to its root table.
It deletes the Color Lookup Table and switches the display into grayscale mode.
It closes the file immediately and displays an error message to the user.
questions.explanation: When the decoder encounters a Clear code (256), it flushes all dynamically learned phrases (258+) and restores the dictionary to its initial pre-populated root state.

chunks.title: Why 9 Bits? Crossing the 256-Entry Boundary
chunks.content_markdown:
Pause for a moment to appreciate a neat binary consequence of adding those new dictionary slots. When our pixels were just raw $$8\text{-bit}$$ palette numbers ($$0$$ through $$255$$), every pixel fit inside $$8\text{ bits}$$ ($$2^8 = 256$$ possible values).

Now, however, our LZW encoder needs to send code numbers that include `256` (Clear), `257` (EOI), `258` (first multi-pixel phrase), `259` (second phrase), and so on! Since $$8\text{ bits}$$ can only count from $$0$$ to $$255$$, $$8\text{ bits}$$ cannot represent code `256` or `258`.

By adding just **$$1$$ extra bit**—moving from $$8\text{ bits}$$ to **$$9\text{ bits}$$** per code—we double the number of addressable slots from $$2^8 = 256$$ to $$2^9 = 512$$ slots (numbered `0` through `511`)! That means a $$256\text{-color}$$ GIF begins transmitting its LZW codes using $$9\text{-bit}$$ chunks, giving the dictionary room for $$254$$ learned multi-pixel phrases (`258` through `511`) before it even needs a tenth bit.

questions.prompt: Why must LZW codewords in a 256-color GIF start at 9 bits wide rather than 8 bits wide?
choices: Telephone modems in 1987 could only transmit binary chunks that were odd multiples of 3 bits.
The 9th bit is required to specify whether each pixel belongs to the top half or bottom half of the screen.
An 8-bit number can only represent 0–255, leaving no room for control codes or learned phrases.
CompuServe used the extra bit to embed a hidden billing timestamp inside every pixel.
questions.explanation: Because 2^8 = 256 covers only indices 0 through 255, at least 9 bits (2^9 = 512 values, 0 through 511) are required to represent codes 256, 257, and newly learned phrases starting at 258.

questions.prompt: How does spending 9 bits on code 258 or 260 still achieve dramatic compression compared to raw 8-bit pixels?
choices: The 9-bit codes are automatically shrunk back down to 2 bits by the user's monitor cable.
The encoder only transmits every ninth code and lets the decoder guess the eight codes in between.
Each 9-bit code also replaces the 768-byte Color Lookup Table at the top of the file.
A single 9-bit code above 257 can replace two, five, or dozens of 8-bit pixels at once.
questions.explanation: Although one 9-bit code is 1 bit wider than a single 8-bit pixel, any dictionary code from 258 upward represents a multi-pixel sequence (2 pixels = 16 bits, 10 pixels = 80 bits, etc.).

chunks.title: Smaller Palettes, Smaller Starting Codes
chunks.content_markdown:
What if a GIF image only uses a $$4\text{-color}$$ palette (slots `0`, `1`, `2`, and `3`, where $$2^2 = 4$$)? Does it still have to waste $$9\text{ bits}$$ on every starting code?

Not in GIF87a! Right before the compressed LZW data begins, the file stores a single byte called the **LZW Minimum Code Size** (let's call it $$L$$). If an image has $$2^L$$ root colors, then:
- Root colors occupy slots $$0$$ through $$2^L - 1$$
- The **Clear code** sits at $$2^L$$
- The **End-of-Information (EOI) code** sits at $$2^L + 1$$
- Learned phrases begin at $$2^L + 2$$, and the starting code width is just $$L + 1\text{ bits}$$!

For example, in a $$4\text{-color}$$ image ($$L = 2$$, since $$2^2 = 4$$), slots `0`–`3` are the four colors, `4` is Clear, `5` is EOI, learned phrases start at slot `6`, and the codes begin at a tiny **$$3\text{ bits}$$** wide ($$2 + 1 = 3\text{ bits}$$)! Now that we know how the starting table is set up, let's hand-trace how LZW actually encodes and decodes a picture.

questions.prompt: If a GIF image uses an LZW Minimum Code Size of L = 4 (meaning 2^4 = 16 root colors, indexed 0–15), what are the code numbers for Clear, End of Information, and the first learned phrase?
choices: Clear = 16, End of Information = 17, and the first learned phrase = 18.
Clear = 256, End of Information = 257, and the first learned phrase = 258.
Clear = 0, End of Information = 1, and the first learned phrase = 2.
Clear = 4, End of Information = 5, and the first learned phrase = 6.
questions.explanation: With 2^4 = 16 root colors occupying indices 0 through 15, the Clear code is placed at 2^4 = 16, End of Information at 17, and the first dynamically learned phrase at 18.

questions.prompt: For that same 16-color GIF (where L = 4), how many bits wide are the initial LZW codes at the start of the stream?
choices: 4 bits wide.
5 bits wide.
8 bits wide.
9 bits wide.
questions.explanation: When the LZW Minimum Code Size is L, the initial code size is L + 1 bits (here 4 + 1 = 5 bits, allowing values 0 through 31) so there is room above 0–15 for control codes and initial learned phrases.

sections.title: 8. Hand-Tracing LZW: Greedy Prefix Matching & Lockstep Decoder Reconstruction
sections.summary: Walk step by step through LZW encoding and decoding on a concrete pixel stream using no higher math. Trace how the encoder accumulates the longest known prefix string $$w$$, emits the code for $$w$$ when the next pixel $$k$$ creates an unseen sequence $$w + k$$, and assigns $$w + k$$ to the next available slot (starting at $$258$$)—while the decoder rebuilds the exact same dictionary one step behind.
introduced_terms: greedy longest-match prefix (w) and extension character (k)
dictionary rule (emit w, register w + k)

chunks.title: The Two Variables of LZW Encoding: Prefix w and Next Pixel k
chunks.content_markdown:
You don't need a computer-science degree to run the LZW encoder by hand—in fact, the entire loop uses just two sticky notes on your desk, traditionally called **$$w$$** and **$$k$$**.

- **$$w$$ (the working prefix):** Holds the sequence of pixels we have accumulated so far that *already exists* in our dictionary.
- **$$k$$ (the extension character):** Holds the very next single pixel we just read from the image.

At every step, the encoder checks its dictionary for the combined sequence **$$w + k$$** (meaning string $$w$$ followed immediately by pixel $$k$$). This is called finding the **greedy longest-match prefix (w) and extension character (k)**:
1. **If $$w + k$$ IS already in the dictionary:** Don't output anything yet! Greedily swallow $$k$$ into your working string (set $$w = w + k$$) and read the next pixel.
2. **If $$w + k$$ is NOT in the dictionary:** We have found the longest match we know (`w`), plus one new pixel (`k`) that makes a brand-new phrase!

questions.prompt: In the LZW encoding loop, what do the variables w and k represent?
choices: w is the longest known prefix string accumulated so far, and k is the next single pixel read from the input.
w is the total width of the image in pixels, and k is the total file size in kilobytes.
w is the white balance of the monitor, and k is the black level of the printer ink.
w is the backward distance in the sliding window, and k is the number of bytes to delete.
questions.explanation: During LZW encoding, w holds the current working prefix (a string already present in the dictionary) and k holds the next single input symbol being tested.

questions.prompt: What does the LZW encoder do when it checks the combined string w + k and finds that w + k IS already in the dictionary?
choices: It immediately outputs the code for w + k and resets the entire dictionary to empty.
It outputs nothing yet, updates w to equal w + k, and reads the next pixel to try for an even longer match.
It discards pixel k as a duplicate error and skips forward to the next scan line.
It outputs the Clear code (256) because the dictionary has encountered a collision.
questions.explanation: LZW is a 'greedy' longest-match algorithm: as long as w + k is already in the dictionary, it keeps extending w without emitting a code until it hits an unseen combination.

chunks.title: The Golden Dictionary Rule: Emit w, Register w + k, Set w = k
chunks.content_markdown:
What happens at the exact moment $$w + k$$ is **not** found in the dictionary? The encoder executes the three-part **dictionary rule (emit w, register w + k)**:

1. **Emit the code for $$w$$:** Write the dictionary code number for the known prefix $$w$$ to the output file.
2. **Register $$w + k$$ in the dictionary:** Write the new combined sequence $$w + k$$ into the next empty dictionary slot (starting at `258` in a $$256\text{-color}$$ GIF).
3. **Reset $$w = k$$:** Don't throw pixel $$k$$ away! Because we only emitted the code for $$w$$, pixel $$k$$ has not been sent to the output file yet. So $$k$$ becomes the starting prefix $$w$$ for the very next step!

Why is Step 3 (`set w = k`) so crucial? Because pixel $$k$$ does double duty: first, it acts as the *ending character* of the new dictionary entry $$w + k$$; second, it acts as the *first character* of the next output token!

questions.prompt: When the LZW encoder discovers that w + k is NOT in the dictionary, what three actions does it perform?
choices: It emits the code for w + k, deletes w from the dictionary, and sets w to empty.
It emits the code for k, registers k + w in the dictionary, and re-reads the previous pixel.
It emits the code for w, adds w + k to the next dictionary slot, and sets w = k.
It emits both w and k as raw bytes, skips a dictionary slot, and advances two pixels.
questions.explanation: When w + k is unseen, the encoder outputs the code for the known prefix w, registers the new string w + k in the next available dictionary slot, and initializes the next prefix w to k.

questions.prompt: Why must the encoder set w = k (rather than setting w to empty) after emitting the code for w?
choices: Because the LZW algorithm requires every output code to begin with the letter k.
Because setting w to empty would trigger an automatic hardware reboot on IBM PCs.
Because pixel k must be transmitted twice in a row to verify phone line quality.
Because only w was emitted to the output stream, so pixel k still needs to be encoded as the start of the next match.
questions.explanation: Since the code emitted only covered the prefix w, the pixel k has not yet been represented in the output stream; setting w = k makes k the starting symbol of the next phrase.

chunks.title: Hand-Tracing the Encoder on a Dithered Pixel Row
chunks.content_markdown:
Let's hand-trace our $$256\text{-color}$$ GIF encoder on a $$7\text{-pixel}$$ dithered stripe of Red (Palette `10`) and White (Palette `20`):
Input pixels: `10, 20, 10, 20, 10, 20, 10` (after an initial Clear code `256`).

Start with the first pixel in $$w$$: **$$w = \text{'10'}$$**.
- **Step 1 (read $$k = \text{'20'}$$):** Is `'10, 20'` in the dictionary? No! Emit code for $$w$$ (**`10`**), add **Slot `258` = `'10, 20'`**, and set $$w = \text{'20'}$$.
- **Step 2 (read $$k = \text{'10'}$$):** Is `'20, 10'` in the dictionary? No! Emit code for $$w$$ (**`20`**), add **Slot `259` = `'20, 10'`**, and set $$w = \text{'10'}$$.
- **Step 3 (read $$k = \text{'20'}$$):** Is `'10, 20'` in the dictionary? **YES—it's Slot `258`!** Swallow it: $$w = \text{'10, 20'}$$.
- **Step 4 (read next $$k = \text{'10'}$$):** Is `'10, 20, 10'` in the dictionary? No! Emit code for $$w$$ (**`258`**), add **Slot `260` = `'10, 20, 10'`**, and set $$w = \text{'10'}$$.
- **Step 5 (read $$k = \text{'20'}$$):** `'10, 20'` is in the dictionary (Slot `258`), so $$w = \text{'10, 20'}$$.
- **Step 6 (read final $$k = \text{'10'}$$):** Is `'10, 20, 10'` in the dictionary? **YES—it's Slot `260`!** Set $$w = \text{'10, 20, 10'}$$. End of input: emit **`260`**!

Our $$7$$ pixels compressed into just $$4$$ tokens: **`10, 20, 258, 260`**!

questions.prompt: In our hand-trace of '10, 20, 10, 20, 10, 20, 10', why didn't the encoder emit a code during Step 3 when it saw the second '10, 20' pair?
choices: Because '10, 20' had just been registered as Slot 258 in Step 1, so the encoder greedily extended w to '10, 20'.
Because the encoder skips every third pixel to save telephone bandwidth.
Because '10, 20' is a reserved CompuServe control code that cannot be transmitted.
Because the dictionary was already full after learning two entries.
questions.explanation: Since Step 1 added '10, 20' to Slot 258, encountering '10' followed by '20' in Step 3 matched an existing entry; the greedy encoder absorbed it into w and read the next pixel to build the 3-pixel entry '10, 20, 10' (Slot 260).

questions.prompt: How many pixels did the single output code '260' represent at the end of our 7-pixel hand-trace?
questions.explanation: Slot 260 was created in Step 4 by combining w = '10, 20' (Slot 258) with k = '10', so emitting code 260 at the end represented the 3-pixel sequence '10, 20, 10'.

chunks.title: How the Decoder Rebuilds the Dictionary One Step Behind
chunks.content_markdown:
Now comes the part that feels like a magic trick when you first see it: **lockstep decoder reconstruction**. Remember, the encoder *only* sent the four numbers **`10, 20, 258, 260`** over the phone line—it never sent the dictionary table!

How can the user's home computer decode `258` and `260`? Watch what happens as the decoder reads **`10, 20, 258, 260`** one code at a time:
1. **Read `10`:** Outputs pixel `'10'`. (Remembers `prev = '10'`).
2. **Read `20`:** Outputs pixel `'20'`. Now the decoder asks: *'Why did the encoder stop after `10` instead of combining `10` with whatever came next?'* Because `10` + the first pixel of the new code (`'20'`) wasn't in the dictionary yet! So the decoder immediately adds **Slot `258` = `'10, 20'`**! (Sets `prev = '20'`).
3. **Read `258`:** The decoder looks up Slot `258`, which it *just created a microsecond ago*! It outputs `'10, 20'`. And since `prev` was `'20'` and the first pixel of `258` is `'10'`, the decoder adds **Slot `259` = `'20, 10'`**! (Sets `prev = '10, 20'`).
4. **Read `260`:** Wait—what happens if a code arrives *before* the decoder has added it? Hold that thought for Section 9; in normal steps, the decoder always reconstructs each slot **one step behind** the encoder!

questions.prompt: During normal LZW decompression, how does the decoder know what new phrase to add to its dictionary each time it receives a new code?
choices: It pauses the modem transfer and asks the CompuServe server to send the definition in plain text.
It takes the string from the previous code and appends the very first pixel of the newly received code.
It adds the numeric values of the last two codes together and divides by 256.
It looks ahead ten codes into the future to see which colors appear most frequently.
questions.explanation: Because the encoder emitted the previous code (w) when w + k wasn't in the dictionary—and then started the current code with k—the character k is guaranteed to be the first pixel of the current code!

questions.prompt: Why is the LZW decoder described as rebuilding the dictionary 'one step behind' the encoder?
choices: The decoder must wait until the entire image file is saved to disk before it can decode the first pixel.
The decoder intentionally delays displaying each row by one second so the monitor does not flicker.
The decoder skips slot 258 and starts numbering its own dictionary entries at slot 259.
The encoder creates a new slot when emitting w, whereas the decoder learns the extension pixel k upon reading the very next code.
questions.explanation: When the encoder emits w, it already knows the next pixel k and registers w + k immediately; the decoder discovers k one step later when it sees the first pixel of the following code.

chunks.title: Why LZW Crushes Both Solid Runs and Dithered Textures
chunks.content_markdown:
Before we examine the famous cliffhanger we just stumbled across at the end of Chunk 4 (`Read 260` when the decoder had only built up to `259`!), let's appreciate what LZW achieves on real images.

- **On solid color streaks** (like `Blue, Blue, Blue, Blue...`), LZW first learns a 2-pixel run (`258 = BB`), then a 3-pixel run (`259 = BBB`), then a 4-pixel run (`260 = BBBB`), growing its streak length every single step so a solid background shrinks down to a tiny handful of codes.
- **On dithered checkerboards and repeating textures** (where Run-Length Encoding completely failed!), LZW effortlessly learns 2-pixel dither pairs (`Red, White`), 4-pixel dither bars (`Red, White, Red, White`), and 8-pixel dither strips.

Wait—go back and look closely at Step 4 of our decoder trace in the previous chunk. When the encoder sent **`10, 20, 258, 260`**, our decoder had built Slot `258` and Slot `259`—and then suddenly received **`260`** before it had created Slot `260`! Did LZW just break? Let's solve that exact mystery in Section 9.

questions.prompt: How do the dictionary entries grow when LZW compresses a long solid streak of identical pixels (such as 'B, B, B, B, B, B...')?
choices: It registers progressively longer runs ('BB', 'BBB', 'BBBB', ...) in successive dictionary slots.
It registers only the 2-pixel pair 'BB' and refuses to create any entries longer than two pixels.
It switches off the dictionary and falls back to sending raw 24-bit RGB triplets.
It combines all consecutive 'B' pixels into a single slot 258 on the very first step.
questions.explanation: On a solid run of 'B's, step 1 registers 'BB' (length 2), step 2 matches 'BB' and registers 'BBB' (length 3), step 3 matches 'BBB' and registers 'BBBB' (length 4), rapidly compressing long streaks.

questions.prompt: What puzzling situation did we encounter at the end of our decoder trace for '10, 20, 258, 260'?
choices: The decoder ran out of memory after creating only two dictionary entries.
The code number 258 was smaller than the Clear code 256, causing a syntax error.
The encoder emitted code 260 on the very step it created Slot 260, before the decoder had registered Slot 260.
The output stream contained more codes than there were original pixels in the image.
questions.explanation: Because the decoder builds each dictionary slot one step behind the encoder, if the encoder uses a brand-new slot on the exact step it was minted, the decoder receives a code number that is not yet in its table!

sections.title: 9. The Famous kwkwk Anomaly: Decoding a Code Before It Exists
sections.summary: Investigate the classic puzzle of LZW decompression: what happens when a repeating pattern causes the encoder to emit a brand-new dictionary code on the very step it was created—one step before the decoder has learned what that code means? See why this edge case only occurs for symmetrical strings of the form $$k\text{w}k\text{w}k$$, and how appending the previous string's first pixel to itself solves the mystery every time.
introduced_terms: LZW exception handler (previous string + first character)

chunks.title: Catching the Encoder in the Act: How Code 260 Arrived Early
chunks.content_markdown:
At the end of Section 8, we caught the LZW encoder doing something that looked almost illegal. On our 7-pixel dithered stripe `10, 20, 10, 20, 10, 20, 10`, the encoder output the four codes **`10, 20, 258, 260`**.

Let's replay the crime scene in slow motion from the decoder's chair:
- After reading `10` and `20`, the decoder creates **Slot `258` = `'10, 20'`**, and remembers `prev = '20'`.
- Next, the decoder reads `258` (`'10, 20'`). It takes `prev` (`'20'`) plus the first pixel of `258` (`'10'`) and creates **Slot `259` = `'20, 10'`**. It sets `prev = '10, 20'` (which is Slot `258`).
- At this exact instant, the highest slot in the decoder's dictionary is **`259`**—and the very next code arriving over the phone line is **`260`**!

This is the famous **kwkwk decoder anomaly (unseen-code edge case)**: the encoder minted Slot `260` (`'10, 20, 10'`) and *immediately* used Slot `260` as its next output token before the decoder had a chance to learn what `260` means!

questions.prompt: What is the 'kwkwk decoder anomaly' (unseen-code edge case) in LZW decompression?
choices: The decoder receives a code number for the very next dictionary slot that it has not yet filled in.
The encoder accidentally emits a negative code number when an image contains pure black pixels.
The decoder's dictionary overflows past 4,096 slots and overwrites the Color Lookup Table.
The encoder sends the End-of-Information code (257) before sending the Clear code (256).
questions.explanation: The kwkwk anomaly occurs when the encoder registers a new dictionary entry and immediately emits that new entry's code on the very next match, so the decoder (working one step behind) sees a code equal to its next unfilled slot.

questions.prompt: In our trace of '10, 20, 258, 260', what is the highest slot number the decoder has defined at the moment code 260 arrives?
choices: Slot 255.
Slot 258.
Slot 259.
Slot 261.
questions.explanation: After reading 10 and 20, the decoder created Slot 258; after reading 258, it created Slot 259. Thus, when code 260 arrives, the decoder's table only has entries up through Slot 259.

chunks.title: The Pattern Behind the Puzzle: Why It's Called kwkwk
chunks.content_markdown:
Why did the encoder create Slot `260` and immediately use it? Let's trace the exact structure required for that to happen.

Suppose the encoder just matched a prefix that starts with a single pixel **$$k$$** followed by some middle string **$$w$$**—so the previous output string was **$$k\text{w}$$** (in our example, Slot `258` was `'10, 20'`, where $$k = \text{'10'}$$ and $$w = \text{'20'}$$).

1. While matching that $$k\text{w}$$, the encoder peeked at the next pixel, saw another **$$k$$** (`'10'`), emitted the code for $$k\text{w}$$ (`258`), and registered the new entry **$$k\text{w}k$$** (`'10, 20, 10'`) in **Slot `260`**.
2. Remember the Golden Rule from Section 8: after emitting $$k\text{w}$$, that extension pixel **$$k$$** becomes the start of the *next* match!
3. If the pixels that immediately follow that $$k$$ happen to be **$$w$$** and **$$k$$** again—forming the 5-part sequence **$$k\text{w}k\text{w}k$$** (`10, 20, 10, 20, 10`)—then the encoder starting at the middle $$k$$ sees $$k\text{w}k$$ (`10, 20, 10`), which is the **exact Slot `260` it just created a microsecond ago**!

questions.prompt: Why does the unseen-code anomaly ONLY occur when the input stream contains an overlapping pattern of the form kwkwk?
choices: Because LZW encoders are programmed to reverse the order of pixels whenever five pixels match.
Because the letter w represents white pixels and the letter k represents black pixels in CMYK printing.
Because telephone modems automatically duplicate every fifth byte when line noise occurs.
Because the final pixel k of the newly registered entry kwk immediately serves as the first pixel of the next match kwk.
questions.explanation: When the encoder sees kw followed by k, it emits kw, registers kwk in the new slot, and starts its next match at that middle k; if w and k immediately follow (forming kwkwk), the new match is kwk—the exact slot just created!

questions.prompt: In our 7-pixel dithered stripe, which 5-pixel substring formed the 'kwkwk' pattern that triggered code 260?
choices: 10, 10, 10, 10, 10 (where k = 10 and w is empty).
10, 20, 30, 40, 50 (where every pixel is distinct).
questions.explanation: Starting at the third pixel of '10, 20, 10, 20, 10, 20, 10', the 5-pixel sequence '10, 20, 10, 20, 10' matches kwkwk with k = 10 and w = 20.

chunks.title: First-Equals-Last Character Symmetry: The Decoder's Clue
chunks.content_markdown:
Put yourself back in the decoder's shoes. You just decoded `prev = '10, 20'` (which was $$k\text{w}$$), and now you receive the mystery code **`260`**—the slot right at the top of your table that you haven't filled in yet!

To fill in Slot `260`, you normally compute:
`Slot 260 = prev + (first pixel of current code)`

Wait—here the current code *is* Slot `260`! How can you know the **first pixel of Slot `260`** before you know what Slot `260` is?

Look at the formula on the line above: `Slot 260 = prev + (first pixel of Slot 260)`.
Since `Slot 260` *starts* with `prev`, the **first pixel of Slot `260`** is guaranteed to be the **first pixel of `prev`**! That gives us **first-equals-last character symmetry**: every unseen-code entry $$k\text{w}k$$ starts with $$k$$ (the first pixel of `prev`) and *also ends* with that exact same pixel $$k$$!

questions.prompt: Why does the decoder already know the FIRST pixel of the mystery unseen code even before looking it up?
choices: Because the mystery slot was built by extending 'prev', so its first pixel must be identical to the first pixel of 'prev'.
Because every dictionary entry above 257 is required by the GIF specification to begin with Palette Slot 0.
Because the encoder sends the first pixel as a separate uncompressed byte inside the file header.
Because the first pixel of any unseen code is always equal to the image's background color.
questions.explanation: Since the new dictionary slot is formed by taking the previous string (prev) and appending one pixel, the new slot begins with prev—meaning its first pixel is simply the first pixel of prev!

questions.prompt: What is 'first-equals-last character symmetry' in any LZW dictionary entry that triggers the unseen-code anomaly?
choices: The unseen entry is always a complete palindrome that reads identically forward and backward.
The unseen entry (kwk) always begins and ends with the exact same pixel value (k).
The unseen entry always contains an even number of pixels totaling at least eight bytes.
The unseen entry always swaps its first and last pixels when displayed on the monitor.
questions.explanation: Because the mystery entry has the form kwk (prev = kw followed by its own first character k), its first character and its last character are always identical (both equal to k).

chunks.title: The One-Line Fix: Previous String + First Character of Previous String
chunks.content_markdown:
That observation gives every LZW decoder a clean, foolproof rescue rule called the **LZW exception handler (previous string + first character)**:

- **Normal Case (code IS in the dictionary):**
  Output `dictionary[code]`, and add `prev + first_pixel(dictionary[code])` to the next slot.
- **Exception Case (code is NOT in the dictionary yet—i.e., `code == next_free_slot`):**
  Construct the string by taking **`prev + first_pixel(prev)`**, output that string, and store it into `dictionary[code]`!

Let's test that rule on our cliffhanger (`Read 260` when `prev = '10, 20'`):
1. Is `260` in the dictionary yet? No (`260 == next_free_slot`)!
2. Take `prev` (`'10, 20'`) and append `first_pixel(prev)` (`'10'`), giving **`'10, 20, 10'`**.
3. Output **`'10, 20, 10'`** and save **Slot `260` = `'10, 20, 10'`**!

Putting all three decoded pieces together—`10`, `20`, `'10, 20'` (`258`), and `'10, 20, 10'` (`260`)—the decoder reconstructs **`10, 20, 10, 20, 10, 20, 10`**, all $$7$$ original pixels bit for bit!

questions.prompt: When an LZW decoder receives a code number equal to its next unfilled dictionary slot, how does its exception handler construct the decoded string?
choices: It takes the previously decoded string (prev) and appends the very last pixel of that previous string.
It repeats the entire previously decoded string (prev) twice in a row.
It outputs a single pixel of color 0 and resets the dictionary to slot 258.
It takes the previously decoded string (prev) and appends the very first pixel of that same previous string.
questions.explanation: In the kwkwk exception case, the missing entry is kwk, where prev = kw and k = first_pixel(prev); thus prev + first_pixel(prev) reconstructs kwk.

questions.prompt: Suppose an LZW decoder just decoded 'prev = Red, Blue, Green' and immediately receives an unseen code for the next unfilled slot. What pixel sequence does that unseen code represent?
choices: Red, Blue, Green, Green.
Red, Blue, Green, Blue.
Red, Blue, Green, Red.
Green, Blue, Red, Green.
questions.explanation: Applying the rule 'prev + first_pixel(prev)' to 'Red, Blue, Green' appends its first pixel ('Red') to the end, yielding 'Red, Blue, Green, Red'.

chunks.title: Why Solid Streaks Trigger kwkwk on the Very First Repeat!
chunks.content_markdown:
Programmers who wrote early GIF decoders in 1987 sometimes forgot to include the `kwkwk` exception handler, assuming it was a rare mathematical curiosity that would almost never happen in real life. Then they opened their very first cartoon or solid-background image—and their program crashed immediately!

Why? Because a simple solid streak of three identical pixels—like `Blue, Blue, Blue`—is actually the simplest `kwkwk` pattern of all (where $$k = \text{Blue}$$ and the middle string $$w$$ is **empty**, so $$k\text{w}k\text{w}k = kkk$$)!

Watch `Blue, Blue, Blue` encode:
1. Start with $$w = \text{'Blue'}$$. Read next `'Blue'`: emit **`Blue`**, register **Slot `258` = `'Blue, Blue'`**, and set $$w = \text{'Blue'}$$.
2. Read the third `'Blue'`, followed by a fourth `'Blue'`: `'Blue, Blue'` matches **Slot `258`**, so the encoder immediately emits **`258`** on Step 2—before the decoder has processed a second code to create Slot `258`!

Thanks to the `prev + first_pixel(prev)` rule, both solid runs (`kkk`) and dithered weaves (`kwkwk`) decode without a hitch. Now let's see how GIF packs these variable-width codes into bytes and streams them over slow modems.

questions.prompt: Why does even a simple solid-color streak like 'Blue, Blue, Blue, Blue' immediately trigger the kwkwk decoder exception?
choices: When the middle string w is empty, kwkwk simplifies to kkk, so the encoder creates 'Blue, Blue' (Slot 258) and uses it on the very next step.
Solid streaks bypass the pre-populated root table (0–255) and start encoding at slot 4,096.
The LZW encoder treats solid blue pixels as Clear codes unless the exception handler is active.
Solid streaks cause the Color Lookup Table to swap the red and blue channels on every odd pixel.
questions.explanation: A solid run of identical pixels is the special case of kwkwk where w is the empty string (making kwk = kk and kwkwk = kkk), causing Slot 258 ('Blue, Blue') to be emitted immediately after 'Blue'.

questions.prompt: What happened to early 1987 hobbyist GIF viewers if the programmer forgot to implement the kwkwk unseen-code exception case?
choices: They still decoded every image perfectly, but took twice as long to calculate the Color Lookup Table.
They crashed or produced corrupted streaks as soon as an image contained solid color runs or repeating textures.
They displayed the image upside down because the scan lines arrived in reverse order.
They automatically converted 256-color photographs into 2-color black-and-white drawings.
questions.explanation: Because solid color runs (kkk) and repeating dither patterns (kwkwk) occur constantly in real graphics, a decoder lacking the unseen-code handler fails almost immediately on everyday GIF files.

sections.title: 10. Variable-Width Bit Packing, 12-Bit Table Resets & Four-Pass Interlacing
sections.summary: Complete the GIF87a architecture by seeing how code numbers start at a compact $$9\text{ bits}$$ wide and widen one bit at a time as the dictionary crosses $$512$$, $$1,024$$, and $$2,048$$ entries up to GIF's $$12\text{-bit}$$ ceiling ($$2^{12} = 4,096$$ slots). Explore how emitting a Clear code resets a full table to adapt to changing image regions, and how four-pass Venetian-blind interlacing let dial-up users preview an entire picture in seconds—setting the stage for GIF89a in Part II.
introduced_terms: 12-bit dictionary ceiling (4,096 entries) and adaptive Clear reset

chunks.title: Variable-Width Bit Packing: Growing from 9 Bits to 12 Bits
chunks.content_markdown:
How large should we let our LZW dictionary grow? In GIF87a, Steve Wilhite set the maximum dictionary size to $$4,096$$ slots (numbered `0` through `4095`). Because $$2^{12} = 4,096$$, addressing all $$4,096$$ slots requires **$$12\text{ bits}$$** per code.

Wait: at the beginning of a $$256\text{-color}$$ image, when the dictionary only has entries up to `258` or `300`, wouldn't sending a full $$12\text{ bits}$$ for every single code waste $$3\text{ bits}$$ of precious modem time on every token?

To avoid that waste, GIF uses **variable-width bit packing (9-bit to 12-bit codes)**:
- **Slots `258` to `511`:** Codes are packed using just **$$9\text{ bits}$$** each ($$2^9 = 512$$).
- **As soon as Slot `511` is filled:** Both encoder and decoder automatically widen to **$$10\text{ bits}$$** per code for slots `512` through `1023` ($$2^{10} = 1,024$$).
- **After Slot `1023`:** Codes widen to **$$11\text{ bits}$$** (`1024` through `2047`, where $$2^{11} = 2,048$$).
- **After Slot `2047`:** Codes widen to **$$12\text{ bits}$$** (`2048` through `4095`, where $$2^{12} = 4,096$$).

These variable-width bit codes are packed tightly head-to-tail across byte boundaries into data sub-blocks of up to $$255\text{ bytes}$$ each, wasting not a single bit.

questions.prompt: Why does a 256-color GIF start with 9-bit LZW codes and gradually widen to 10, 11, and 12 bits rather than using 12-bit codes from the very beginning?
choices: Using narrower 9-bit and 10-bit codes early on saves bandwidth while the dictionary still has fewer than 512 or 1,024 entries.
Telephone modems need several seconds to warm up before they can transmit 12-bit numbers reliably.
The first 512 pixels of every GIF image are required to be monochrome black-and-white.
Computer monitors draw the top quarter of the screen with 9-bit color and the bottom quarter with 12-bit color.
questions.explanation: While the dictionary has fewer than 512 entries (slots 0–511), every code fits inside 9 bits; sending 12 bits per code from the start would waste 3 bits on every early token.

questions.prompt: In a 256-color GIF, at what dictionary slot threshold do the LZW codewords step up from 9 bits wide to 10 bits wide?
choices: As soon as the dictionary fills slot 255 and needs to address slot 256.
As soon as the dictionary fills slot 511 and needs to address slot 512.
As soon as the dictionary fills slot 1,023 and needs to address slot 1,024.
As soon as the dictionary fills slot 4,095 and needs to address slot 4,096.
questions.explanation: A 9-bit unsigned integer can represent values 0 through 511 (2^9 = 512 slots); once slot 511 is created, the next code could be 512, so both encoder and decoder step up to 10-bit codes.

chunks.title: The 12-Bit Ceiling (4,096 Slots) and Adaptive Clear Resets
chunks.content_markdown:
Why did GIF87a cap the dictionary at a **12-bit dictionary ceiling (4,096 entries) and adaptive Clear reset** instead of letting codes grow to $$15$$ or $$16\text{ bits}$$ ($$65,536$$ slots)?

Remember our 1987 hardware constraints from Section 3: a Commodore 64 had only $$64\text{ KB}$$ of total system RAM! A $$4,096\text{-slot}$$ table fit comfortably inside a few kilobytes of memory on every 8-bit and 16-bit home computer, whereas a $$65,536\text{-slot}$$ table would have blown right past an 8-bit microcomputer's memory limits.

What happens when a complex photograph fills all $$4,096$$ slots (up through Slot `4095`) halfway down the image? Suppose the top half of the picture was blue sky and puffy clouds, so all $$4,096$$ slots are full of sky phrases—and suddenly the scan lines reach green forest trees and brown bark!

Whenever the table fills up (or compression efficiency drops because the scene's texture changed), the encoder simply emits the **Clear code (`256`)**! Both sides instantly wipe slots `258`–`4095`, drop the code size back down to a nimble **$$9\text{ bits}$$**, and start learning fresh forest phrases from scratch.

questions.prompt: Why did Steve Wilhite cap GIF's LZW dictionary at 12 bits (2^12 = 4,096 entries) rather than 16 bits (65,536 entries)?
choices: Terry Welch's 1984 algorithm mathematically breaks down if a dictionary ever exceeds 4,096 entries.
Images in 1987 were prohibited from containing more than 4,096 total pixels on screen.
A 4,096-entry table easily fit inside the scarce RAM of 1980s home computers while still delivering strong compression.
CompuServe's mainframe hard drives used 12-bit sectors and could not store larger numbers.
questions.explanation: Keeping the dictionary capped at 4,096 slots allowed even memory-constrained 1980s microcomputers (like the 64 KB Commodore 64 or Apple II) to decode GIF files quickly in RAM.

questions.prompt: What two things happen when a GIF encoder emits a Clear code (256) after filling its 4,096-slot dictionary halfway through an image?
choices: The top half of the picture is erased from the monitor AND the Color Lookup Table is deleted.
The codeword bit width increases to 13 bits AND the modem speed doubles to 2400 baud.
The decoder stops reading the file AND fills the remaining scan lines with solid black.
Learned slots (258–4095) are wiped clean AND the codeword bit width drops from 12 bits back to 9 bits.
questions.explanation: Emitting a Clear code (256) flushes all learned multi-pixel entries (258–4095) so the table can adapt to new image textures, and resets the code width from 12 bits back to the initial 9 bits.

chunks.title: The Dial-Up User's Frustration: Waiting for the Bottom of the Picture
chunks.content_markdown:
With an $$8\text{-bit}$$ Color Lookup Table and $$9\text{-to-}12\text{-bit}$$ LZW compression working together, a $$640 \times 480$$ color picture that once weighed $$921\text{ kilobytes}$$ (taking over two hours at $$1200\text{ baud}$$) shrank down to roughly $$30\text{ to }60\text{ kilobytes}$$—a $$4\text{-to-}8\text{ minute}$$ download!

Yet even a $$5\text{-minute}$$ download had a frustrating human problem. Normally, a raster image is stored in strict top-to-bottom order: Row `0`, Row `1`, Row `2`, all the way down to Row `479`.

Imagine paying CompuServe $$12.50\text{ dollars per hour}$$ while downloading a portrait or weather map from top to bottom. For the first two minutes, all you see creeping down the top of your monitor is empty blue sky or the top of a hat! You have no idea whether the main subject in the center of the frame is what you actually wanted until three or four minutes of connect time have already been billed.

questions.prompt: Why was standard top-to-bottom scan-line transmission frustrating for dial-up users paying by the minute in 1987?
choices: Users had to wait through minutes of top background rows before seeing whether the central subject was what they wanted.
Top-to-bottom transmission caused cathode-ray monitors to overheat along their upper glass edge.
LZW compression could only compress the bottom half of an image when rows were sent in normal order.
Telephone modems lost synchronization whenever more than ten consecutive sky rows were transmitted.
questions.explanation: When an image downloads strictly row by row from top to bottom over a slow modem, the viewer sees only the top border or sky for the first several minutes before the main subject appears.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much did combining an 8-bit palette with LZW compression shrink a typical 640 x 480 color image compared to raw 24-bit true color?
choices: From ~900 kilobytes down to exactly 12 bytes.
From ~900 kilobytes down to roughly 30 to 60 kilobytes.
From ~900 kilobytes down to 890 kilobytes.

questions.explanation: Cutting 3 bytes per pixel to 1 byte (307 KB) and applying LZW dictionary compression typically reduced a 640 x 480 graphic to roughly 30–60 KB, turning a two-hour transfer into a few minutes.

chunks.title: Four-Pass Interlacing: The Venetian-Blind Preview
chunks.content_markdown:
To let dial-up users judge an entire picture within seconds, GIF87a introduced an optional feature called **four-pass interlacing (Venetian-blind progressive rendering)**. Instead of storing rows sequentially (`0, 1, 2, 3, 4...`), an interlaced GIF scrambles the row order into four progressive passes across the whole canvas:

- **Pass 1 ($$\frac{1}{8}$$ of the image):** Sends every **$$8\text{th}$$ row** starting at Row `0` (`0, 8, 16, 24...`). After just $$12.5\%$$ of the download time, the user sees a complete—though blocky—top-to-bottom sketch of the entire picture!
- **Pass 2 (another $$\frac{1}{8}$$):** Fills in every **$$8\text{th}$$ row** halfway between Pass 1, starting at Row `4` (`4, 12, 20, 28...`). Now $$25\%$$ of the rows are on screen (every $$4\text{th}$$ row).
- **Pass 3 ($$\frac{1}{4}$$ of the image):** Fills in every **$$4\text{th}$$ row** starting at Row `2` (`2, 6, 10, 14...`), bringing the picture to $$50\%$$ (all even-numbered rows).
- **Pass 4 (final $$\frac{1}{2}$$):** Fills in all remaining **odd-numbered rows** (`1, 3, 5, 7...`), snapping the image into crisp focus like opening a set of Venetian blinds!

questions.prompt: In GIF87a's four-pass interlacing scheme, which scan lines are transmitted during Pass 1, and what fraction of the total rows do they represent?
choices: Every 8th row starting at row 0 (0, 8, 16, ...), representing 1/8 (12.5 percent) of the image.
Every 2nd row starting at row 1 (1, 3, 5, ...), representing 1/2 (50 percent) of the image.
The top 100 rows in sequential order, representing 1/4 (25 percent) of the image.
Only the four outer border rows of the canvas, representing less than 1 percent of the image.
questions.explanation: Pass 1 transmits every 8th scan line starting at line 0 (0, 8, 16, 24...), allowing the viewer to see a coarse full-height preview after just 1/8 (12.5%) of the rows have arrived.

questions.prompt: Which scan lines are transmitted during the fourth and final pass (Pass 4) of an interlaced GIF?
choices: Every 8th row starting at row 4 (4, 12, 20, ...), comprising 1/8 of the image.
Every 4th row starting at row 2 (2, 6, 10, ...), comprising 1/4 of the image.
All odd-numbered rows (1, 3, 5, 7, ...), comprising the remaining 1/2 of the image.
A duplicate copy of row 0 to verify that no phone line errors occurred.
questions.explanation: After Passes 1, 2, and 3 have filled in all even-numbered scan lines (multiples of 8, plus 4, plus 2), Pass 4 transmits every odd-numbered row (1, 3, 5, 7...), which makes up the final 50% of the image.

chunks.title: The Trade-Off of Interlacing—and the Eve of GIF89a
chunks.content_markdown:
There is one subtle catch to GIF interlacing: an interlaced GIF is often **slightly larger** (by a few percent) than the exact same image saved without interlacing! Why? Because adjacent rows (`Row 0` and `Row 1`) are much more similar to each other than rows separated by an $$8\text{-pixel}$$ jump (`Row 0` and `Row 8`). Skipping $$8$$ rows at a time in Pass 1 slightly disrupts the smooth row-to-row patterns that the LZW dictionary loves to exploit—a small price many users gladly paid for an instant preview.

By late 1988, Steve Wilhite's GIF87a had conquered the dial-up world. For the first time in computing history, an Apple II, Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, Macintosh, and IBM PC could all download and display the exact same full-color graphics file in minutes.

Yet users were already asking for more: *What if a GIF could have transparent backgrounds so sprites could float over any screen? What if a single GIF file could play timed animations?* And lurking quietly beneath Terry Welch's 1984 LZW paper was a sleeping legal time bomb—a software patent owned by Unisys—that would ignite the greatest format war in Internet history. We will explore all of that in **Part II**!

questions.prompt: Why does enabling four-pass interlacing often make a GIF file slightly larger in byte size than a non-interlaced GIF of the exact same picture?
choices: Interlaced GIFs are required to store four separate copies of the 768-byte Color Lookup Table.
Interlacing disables the LZW dictionary completely and reverts to uncompressed 24-bit RGB pixels.
Pass 4 transmits every odd-numbered row twice to prevent Venetian-blind flicker on the monitor.
Jumping 8 rows at a time reduces similarity between consecutive scan lines, slightly lowering LZW compression efficiency.
questions.explanation: Because adjacent scan lines (e.g., row 0 and row 1) usually share stronger visual continuity than rows 8 lines apart (row 0 and row 8), reordering rows for interlacing slightly reduces LZW pattern matches across row boundaries.

questions.prompt: Looking back across all ten sections of Part I, how do GIF87a's three core pillars—indexed palettes, LZW compression, and interlacing—work together?
choices: The 8-bit CLUT discards half the rows, LZW converts the rest into vector formulas, and interlacing encrypts the file for CompuServe.
The 8-bit CLUT cuts pixels to 1 byte, LZW losslessly compresses repeating and dithered patterns, and interlacing provides a fast full-frame dial-up preview.
The 8-bit CLUT provides 16.7 million simultaneous colors, LZW blurs background details lossily, and interlacing doubles the modem baud rate.
The 8-bit CLUT copies IBM CGA memory directly, LZW counts only single-pixel streaks like RLE, and interlacing rotates the image 90 degrees.
questions.explanation: GIF87a solved the 1980s cross-platform and dial-up graphics bottleneck by combining a hardware-independent 8-bit Color Lookup Table (1 byte/pixel), lossless 9-to-12-bit LZW dictionary compression, and optional four-pass interlacing.
